evidence.label: Deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs in every fixed degree

headline: A fixed recipe builds networks with best-possible mixing, in every degree and every large even size.
scope: The result covers every fixed degree of at least 3 and every large enough even number of points. The running time is polynomial in the size, with a power that may depend on the degree.
plain: A Ramanujan graph is a network whose mixing is as good as a large network can get. Earlier recipes built them only for special degrees, or only in the two-team bipartite form, or with a small error. This paper claims an algorithm that builds non-bipartite ones for every degree and every large even size. There is no Lean formalization.
doesNot: This does not give a running time that stays polynomial as the degree grows.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak, and Margulis, with arithmetic constructions
scorecard.significanceWhy: It removes the last error term from explicit constructions of a central object in network design.

explanation:
Take the Petersen graph: ten points, each joined to exactly three others, fifteen links in all. Write its links as a 10-by-10 table of 0s and 1s. That table has ten special numbers called eigenvalues. Roughly, they describe how a signal spreads through the network. The largest is always 3, the number of links at each point. For Petersen the other nine are 1, five times, and −2, four times.

Those other nine numbers measure mixing. When all of them are small, links spread out evenly, with no hidden bottleneck or clump[1]. How small can they be? For networks with d links at each point, the best possible cutoff for large networks is 2√(d − 1)[2]. For d = 3 that is about 2.83. Networks whose other eigenvalues all stay inside −2.83 to 2.83 are called Ramanujan graphs. Petersen qualifies, since 1 and −2 both fit.

The negative side matters too. A cube's corners and edges form another network with three links per point. Its eigenvalues are 3, then 1 and −1 three times each, then −3. The −3 shows that the cube is bipartite: its points split into two teams, and every link joins the two teams. Bipartite networks always break the negative side. A network that meets both sides of the cutoff is connected and not bipartite[3].

Building large Ramanujan graphs on purpose has been hard. In the 1980s, Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak, and separately Margulis, used number theory to build them[4]. Those methods work only for special degrees. Morgenstern extended them to every degree one more than a prime power, including non-bipartite ones[5]. But they never covered every degree and every large size at once[6]. In 2015, Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava built bipartite Ramanujan graphs in every degree[7]. Bipartite graphs get the negative side for free by symmetry. Other fast constructions in every degree allowed a small extra error above the cutoff[8].

Random networks almost work. A random network with d links per point nearly meets the cutoff, with probability tending to one[10]. It meets the exact cutoff about 69 percent of the time in the limit[11]. So such graphs exist. But a random draw needs a check, and the method gives no fixed recipe.

This paper claims a fixed recipe[12]. For every degree d of at least 3, an algorithm takes any large enough even number n. It outputs a network with n points and d links per point. Every eigenvalue other than d lies strictly inside the cutoff on both sides. The running time grows like a power of n, but that power may depend on d. The result covers only large even sizes, and it does not claim a speed that is also polynomial in d[13].

The single difficulty is precision. Getting within a small error of the cutoff was already possible. Removing that error means controlling eigenvalues on a far finer scale, near both ends of the range at once[9]. The main tool is an edge switch[14]. It deletes two links and adds two new ones on the same four points, so every point keeps its d links. But knowing only the overall size of the eigenvalues does not tell how one switch moves them[15]. So the construction tracks extra local information at each point, and makes only switches whose effect it can predict.

The paper also says what it does not do. A related question, the Bilu–Linial conjecture, asks about doubling any network with a sign on each link. This construction does not settle it[16].

How sure is this? The paper has no Lean formalization listed. The theorem is a claim in a long preprint, and no specialist review of it has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proof holds. The claim rests on a long preprint with no Lean formalization and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: A network where every point has the same number of links, called the degree.
One of the special numbers of the network's table of links; together they describe how signals spread through it.
A regular network whose eigenvalues, other than the degree, all lie within 2√(d − 1) of zero.
Split into two teams so that every link joins opposite teams.
Deleting two links and adding two new ones on the same four points, so every degree stays the same.
A running time that grows like a fixed power of the input size.

claims.text: Small nonconstant eigenvalues make the edges of a regular graph spread close to uniformly.
claims.sourceLine: regular graph close to the uniform-density prediction, and thus connect
claims.sourceQuote: Nonconstant adjacency eigenvalues that are small in absolute value make the edge distribution of a regular graph close to the uniform-density prediction, and thus connect spectral estimates to expansion \cite{Alon1986}.

claims.text: The Alon–Boppana bound makes 2√(d−1) asymptotically optimal.
claims.sourceLine: tree; the Alon--Boppana bound makes it asymptotically optimal
claims.sourceQuote: Here $2\sqrt{d-1}$ is the spectral radius of the infinite $d$-regular tree; the Alon--Boppana bound makes it asymptotically optimal \cite{Alon1986,Nilli1991}.

claims.text: The bound forces the graph to be connected and nonbipartite.
claims.sourceLine: also forces $G$ to be connected and nonbipartite.
claims.sourceQuote: Since $d>2\sqrt{d-1}$ for $d\ge3$, this bound also forces $G$ to be connected and nonbipartite.

claims.sourceQuote: These exact constructions do not cover every fixed degree and every prescribed large order simultaneously.

claims.sourceQuote: For bipartite graphs, spectral symmetry also controls the negative edge, yielding simple bipartite Ramanujan families in every degree \cite[Theorems~5.3 and~5.5]{MSS2015}.

claims.text: Earlier deterministic constructions in every degree leave a positive spectral error.
claims.sourceLine: These constructions leave a positive spectral error.
claims.sourceQuote: These constructions leave a positive spectral error.

claims.sourceLine: much finer scale of their distances from both tree edges.
